text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation: Neff v. Patry et al

2004 BCSC 1328

Date:
20041014

Docket:
97-3819

Registry: Victoria

Between:

BARRIE NEFF

Plaintiff

And:

LINDA PATRY also known as LINDA
KELSO

TERRY DIANE ANDERSON also known as
TERRY DIANE LAMING

Defendants

Before:
Master Keighley

Oral Reasons for Judgment

In Chambers

September
16, 2004

Counsel for the Plaintiff:

D.
Rivers (as agent for J. Legh)

Counsel for the Defendant Patry:

D.
Farquhar, Q.C.

Place of Trial/Hearing:

Victoria,
B.C.

[
1
]

THE COURT:
This
is an application by the defendant, Linda Patry, for an order that the Further Amended
Statement of Claim filed July 31, 2002, be struck, or that alternatively,
insofar as claims advanced therein may be barred by expiration of the limitation
period, that they be dismissed.  The motion does not refer to costs, but I
assume that costs are: A issue.

[
2
]

The application is brought pursuant to Rule
19(24) of the
Rules of Court
which reads as follows:

(24) At any stage of a proceeding the court may
order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an endorsement,
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a) it discloses no reasonable claim or defence
as the case may be,

(b) it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or
vexatious,

(c) it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the
fair trial or hearing or the proceeding, or

(d) it is otherwise an abuse of the process of
the court,

and the court may grant judgment or order the
proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may order the costs of the application
to be paid as special costs.

[
3
]

Mr. Farquhar suggests that Rule 19(24)(a) and
(d) are the appropriate provisions with respect to this application.  Rule 19
may be utilized to strike out claims on the basis of effluxion of time:
Mcwilliams
v. Reid Properties
, an unreported decision from the Vancouver Supreme
Court Registry, No. C773202, dating from November 7, 1978.

[
4
]

I note the case of
Miller v. Wolfe
,

[1897] 30 N.S.R. 277
, a decision of the Nova Scotia Court of Appeal, which holds
that the effect of a limitation date is not to destroy, but merely to bar a
cause of action.  Thus, it was decided in the case of
Canadian Pacific
Ltd. v. B.C. Hydro and Power
,
1978 CanLII 398 (BC CA)
, [1979] 10 B.C.L.R. 6, that a cause of
action which still exists but which may be barred by the passage of a
limitation date is not,
ipso facto
, "unnecessary, scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious."

[
5
]

It appears that the plaintiff and Linda Patry
first dealt with each other in 1992, when the plaintiff, then sitting as a
residential tenancy arbitrator, made a ruling in a claim which involved Ms.
Patry as a landlord.  This decision triggered a series of unfortunate events,
which resulted, in part, in this lawsuit, which in its original form advanced
various claims in tort against the defendant Patry and others.  It did not,
however, include allegations of defamation.

[
6
]

The statement of claim was amended in 1998, and
further amended on July 31, 2002.  It was this further amended statement of
claim which for the first time advanced a defamation claim against Patry and
Anderson, the only remaining defendants, and which accounts for this
application.

[
7
]

Indeed, it triggered, on September 24, 2002, an
application by Ms. Patry's then counsel for dismissal of the defamation claims
as being statute-barred or negated by privilege.  This application was heard by
Master McCallum.

[
8
]

It is worthy of note that neither defendant at
that point had raised the limitation issue in their defences: the Further Amended
Statement of Claim having been delivered only a couple of months before.
Master McCallum dismissed the application, indicating that the issue of
privilege could be fully explored at a hearing and, possibly in error, that the
court might be moved to explore the postponement of the limitation date in
appropriate circumstances.  I say “possibly in error” in light of the findings
in the
Zanetti
case.

[
9
]

Mr. Legh takes the position that the essence of
this application is
res judicata
and that the issue has been resolved in
favour of his client.  Mr. Farquhar says that the limitation issue has now been
raised in his client's amended defence and that further evidence has been
obtained by virtue of the plaintiff's disclosure which was not available at the
time of the hearing before Master McCallum.

[
10
]

I agree that in light of these circumstances, when hearing the
application with respect to the limitation issue, a trial court on the basis of
appropriate evidence could grant the relief sought, and I cannot see how I, on
the basis of additional evidence and with the limitation defence now an issue,
cannot do the same on this application.

[
11
]

Master McCallum did not deal with the other issue raised by Mr.
Farquhar, namely, the argument that the pleading cannot be maintained under
Rule 19(24).  On last issue, Mr. Farquhar's position is, essentially, as
follows:

(1)

The allegations in paragraphs 10 and 11 of the
further amended statement of claim are barred by statute.

(2)

Paragraphs 10 and 11 are deficient as pleadings
and disclose no reasonable claim against his client.

[
12
]

On the first point, Mr. Farquhar says that in all pleadings filed to
date and in response to demands for particulars, the statements alleged to have
been made, whatever the precise wording used, were made between January 1992
and September 1998.  As such, he says, the claims are barred by s. 3(2)(c) of
the limitation date, as claims for defamation must be brought within two years
of the date such cause of action arose.  As the allegations of defamation were
raised for the first time in the further amended statement of claim filed in
July 2002, the limitation date, he says, has long passed.

[
13
]

On the second point, Mr. Farquhar says that none of the pleadings
filed or disclosures made to date specify any precise words alleged to have
been used by the defendants or either of them.  Mr. Farquhar refers to the case
of
Bulkley Nechako Cable Vision Ltd. v. CKPG Television Ltd.
, a
decision of the British Columbia Supreme Court emanating from the Prince George
Registry,
[1982] B.C.J. No. 1640
: a decision of then Justice Hardinge sitting
as a local judge of the Supreme Court.  I will quote from paragraph 5 in that
decision and subsequent paragraphs:

5      It was common ground between counsel
that in an action for damages for defamation, the law generally requires that
the plaintiff must include in his pleadings the actual words alleged to have
been spoken of him by the defendant and that it is not enough merely to plead
an allegedly defamatory inference from unspecified words.  It was also conceded
by counsel on behalf of the plaintiffs that the Statement of Claim, as
presently framed, does not comply with the general rule.

6      On behalf of the plaintiffs, Mr.
Hansford drew to my attention a number of English and Canadian decisions in
which the courts of both countries have, in a limited number of instant
permitted a plaintiff to depart from strict compliance with the general rule.
Although the conditions in which a plaintiff may sometimes be permitted to
circumvent the rule seems to be substantially the same in each case, two rather
different means of doing so have emerged.

7      In one line of cases the courts have
held that, in circumstances (to which I shall shortly refer) a plaintiff may
before pleading, require the defendant to supply by way of answer to
interrogatories the words he has published.  Such a way of proceeding was first
sanctioned by the English Court of Appeal in Atkinson v. Fosbroke (1866) L.R.
1
Q.B. 628
, and by the House of Lords, in Russell and Another v. Stubbs, Ltd.

[1913] 2 K.B. 205
.  In our own Court of Appeal the same practice was followed
in Shannon v. King [1931] 2 W.W.R. 963.

8      Our Rules of Court specifically state
that leave is not required for a plaintiff to serve interrogatories after the
expiration of time for delivery of the Statement of Defence (see:  Rule
29(3)).  However I do not interpret that rule as precluding a plaintiff from
being granted leave at an earlier stage of the proceedings in circumstances
where the court is persuaded that it is necessary to do so to secure the just,
speedy and inexpensive determination of a proceeding on its merits as
contemplated by Rule 1(5).

9      The second procedure adopted by some
Canadian courts for avoiding the consequences of the strict application of the
general rule is to permit, in the same circumstances as interrogatories would
presumably be permitted, the plaintiff to set out in his Statement of Claim as
nearly as he can what, allegedly defamatory, words the defendant has
published.  When the pleadings are closed the plaintiff may then examine the
defendant for discovery.  If on being examined for discovery the defendant
admit to having published different or additional words that the plaintiff
believes are defamatory, the plaintiff is then permitted to amend this
Statement of Claim to plead the words the defendant has admitted publishing.

10      Earlier in these reasons I mentioned
that whenever the courts in either this County or England have seen fit to
relax the rule that a plaintiff in an action for defamation must plead the
actual words alleged to have been uttered by him, a special circumstance must
exist.  That circumstance is when the plaintiff does not know and has no means
of ascertaining the exact terms of the allegedly defamatory words except by
extracting them from the defendant.

[
14
]

In the result, Justice Hardinge determined that the case was an
appropriate one in which to strike the pleading for non-compliance with Rule
19(24), and quoting from paragraph 15 he said:

It is unfortunate from the plaintiffs'
viewpoint that, by the operation of the provisions of the Limitation Act,
R.S.B.C., Chap. 736, they may now be faced with further and, perhaps,
insurmountable difficulties.  I am unable to say, as did Meredith J. in Bremer
v. Barrett and Dailly (1975)
1975 CanLII 1081 (BC SC)
, 59 D.L.R. (3d) 618 at 620 that, "The
plaintiffs' dilemma is eased perhaps by the fact that he will be able to
examine Mr. Barrett for discovery and thus perhaps determine --- what was said
[by the defendant Dailly]".  However, this is not a problem with which I
may properly concern myself on the present applications.

[
15
]

Mr. Farquhar points out that there is nothing in the pleadings or
the material before this court or in the responses to requests for particulars
which indicates in any way that the plaintiff has no means of ascertaining the
exact terms of the alleged defamatory words except by extracting them from the
defendant.  However harsh the result he says, given the passing of the
limitation period, that is in fact a necessary consequence.

[
16
]

I have also considered the other authorities referred to by Mr.
Farquhar and in fact referred to in the
Bulkley
case: the case of

Shannon v. King
, [1931] 2 W.W.R. 963, a decision of the British
Columbia Court of Appeal, and the decision of
Isaac v. Guardian Capital
Group Ltd.,

2004 BCSC 254 (CanLII)
, [2004] B.C.J. No. 360, a decision of Justice Melnick.

[
17
]

Mr. Legh says that Rule 19(24) is designed to grant the court
authority to stay those actions which have no chance of success at trial.  He
refers in his written submission to the following authorities:
Bank of
Montreal v. Peddle
,
1998 CanLII 29736 (AB QB)
, [1998] 214 A.R. 85 (Q.B.), which lists eight
principles to be applied in relation to the Alberta equivalent of our Rule
19(24).  He also refers to the decision in
Braun Investment Group Inc. v.
Emco Investment Corp.,

1984 CanLII 266 (BC SC)
, [1984] 58 B.C.L.R. 396, as authority for the
proposition that before pleadings are struck, it must be plain and obvious that
the claim cannot succeed.  If the matter is obscure or raises an arguable
issue, then a motion to strike should be dismissed.

[
18
]

He quotes from the decision of
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.,

[1992] S.C.R. 959, at paragraph 33 as follows:

Thus, the test in Canada governing the
application of provisions like Rule 19(24)(a) of the British Columbia Rules of
Court is. . .assuming that the facts as stated in the statement of claim can be
proved, is it "plain and obvious" that the plaintiff's statement of
claim discloses no reasonable cause of action? As in England, if there is a
chance that the plaintiff might succeed, then the plaintiff should not be
"driven from the judgment seat". Neither the length and complexity of
the issues, the novelty of the cause of action, nor the potential for the
defendant to present a strong defence should prevent the plaintiff from
proceeding with his or her case. Only if the action is certain to fail because
it contains a radical defect ranking with the others listed in 19(24) of the
British Columbia Rules of Court should the relevant portions of a plaintiff's
statement of claim be struck out under Rule 19(24)(a).

[
19
]

Mr. Legh cites the decision in
Horton Bay Holdings Ltd. v.
Wilks
,
[1991] 3 C.P.C. (3d) 112
, for the proposition that there is no
basis for striking a pleading if it may be amended to disclose a reasonable
claim.  He refers to the case of
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v.
Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266, as authority for
the propositions: 1)That any doubt on the plain and obvious test must be
resolved in favour of permitting a pleading to stand.  2)The court must proceed
on the assumption that all facts pleaded are true.  3)The sole question for the
court to determine is if the facts disclose a cause of action.  4)The court
must also determine if the facts as alleged, if proved, would be sufficient to
make out malice if the defendant used the occasion at issue for some wrong or
improper purpose or indirect motive.  5)Regardless of how outrageous or
unfounded this allegation may appear, if the court finds that it assists in
proving the plaintiff's case, it should not be struck.

[
20
]

Mr. Legh also refers to the case of
Fullowka v. Whitford
,

1996 CanLII 10199 (NWT CA)
, [1997] 147 D.L.R. (4th) 531, a decision of the Northwest Territories Court of
Appeal, from which he quotes at page 11:

If a plaintiff pleads facts, she need not have
any evidence of them.  She may rely on later discovery or cross-examination at
trial to yield them.  A plaintiff who is knocked unconscious in a traffic
accident and suffers temporary amnesia may know nothing about the accident.
All of her statement of claim may be speculative assumptions.  But no one would
strike it out on that ground, and her speculations may well be proved accurate
at the trial.

The simple answer is that the Rules and the
decided cases say that a claim should be struck out only for clear want of a
cause of action, or very clear very bad abuse of process.  The remedy for want
of particulars is a demand for particulars, and then (if that is not answered)
a motion for particulars.  The court always has the power to order further
particulars, but to defer giving them until after discovery.  Such a power is completely
inconsistent with the idea that the pleading is liable to be struck out for
mere want of particulars.

[
21
]

None of these authorities address the relatively narrow issue framed
by Mr. Farquhar, namely, that the pleading alleging defamation must be struck
if the precise words complained of are not set out, unless the plaintiff is
able to rely on the exception referred to in the
Bulkley Valley

case, namely, that he can only ascertain the precise words from the defendant
either by interrogatories or discovery.

[
22
]

The plaintiff has raised neither of these exceptions.  On this
basis, the pleadings alleged in paragraphs 10 and 11 cannot stand and must be
struck as disclosing no reasonable claim against this defendant.

[
23
]

Were it not for these deficiencies, I would strike the pleadings in
any event as being statute-barred by virtue of the
Limitation Act
.

[
24
]

Mr. Legh urges me to find that suggestions as to the possibility of
a defamation claim are to be found in the original statement of claim filed in
1992 --

[
25
]

MR. FARQUHAR:  1997.

[
26
]

THE COURT:  Sorry.  1997.  Thank you, Mr. Farquhar -- likely in
paragraph 12 which alleges that both of the present defendants made false
statements to the police.

[
27
]

Pleadings must state in clear and concise terms the facts upon which
a claim is advanced sufficient to allow a defendant to meet that claim.  I
cannot read the allegations contained in the original statement of claim as
indicating to the defendants that the claim in defamation was being advanced.
I also note that a claim may be false and not defamatory.  I find that the
defendants first received notice of a possible claim of defamation on receipt
of the further amended statement of claim in July 2002, well after the
expiration of any limitation date suggested by the evidence.

[
28
]

Finally, Mr. Legh points to the authority represented by
Murphy
v. Kenting Drilling Co. Ltd.
,
[1996] A.J. No. 920
, which provides that
a court should be loathe to strike out a portion of a claim where the matter is
likely to go to trial in any case.  Mr. Legh indicates that this matter will be
proceeding to trial.  As a general rule, the proposition set forth in
Murphy

is the law insofar as that decision relates to applications under Rule 19(24).

[
29
]

However, for the reasons I have indicated, the plaintiff's claims
insofar as they relate to defamation are bound to fail, and I would be loth to
see unnecessary time expended on pursuit of these issues at trial.

[
30
]

Costs?

[
31
]

MR. FARQUHAR:  Well, Your Honour, because this decision disposes of
a large part of the claim with finality, I would ask for costs in any event.

[
32
]

MS. RIVERS:  Certainly I would submit, Your Honour, that this was an
arguable case regardless of the final outcome, and we would be asking for costs
in the cause.

[
33
]

THE COURT:  Rule 19(24) contains a specific reference to the
possibility of awarding the costs of the application and special costs.  Do you
have anything to say with respect to that, Mr. Farquhar?

[
34
]

MR. FARQUHAR:  I would simply suggest this, that Mr. Legh in his
materials submitted that an appropriate sum should he have succeeded would be
the sum of a thousand dollars.  I share that view.  I will not argue with him
on that point.  I would suggest that that would be a reasonable sum in these
circumstances.

[
35
]

THE COURT:  Very well.  The defendant, Patry, will have the costs of
this application set at $1,000.  Thank you both.

[
36
]

MR. FARQUHAR:  Thank you, Your Honour.

[
37
]

MS. RIVERS:  Thank you, Your Honour.

“Master
P. Keighley”
